Nolan set out to make a film about the atomic bomb, working inside a framework that all but guarantees certain choices: the female characters stay thin, and the American establishment — despite building and deploying the most destructive weapon ever used — ends up framed as the aggrieved party. Three hours built around one event, and we never see that event’s human cost. No Hiroshima, no Nagasaki. What we get is Trinity shot with dread, and a hallucination of burned bodies mid-celebration — real craft, but it’s guilt filtered through Oppenheimer’s psychology, not the people who actually died. “We only see what we’re shown” isn’t a defence, it’s the problem — every war film would look blameless in its own cinema by that logic. This isn’t unique to Nolan either; American war films (Iraq, Korea, Vietnam) keep casting the US as victim in wars it started, the same way some WWII films let American soldiers alone liberate the camps and quietly cut the Soviets out. To be fair, the film’s real subject is different: Oppenheimer devoured by the establishment that used him. That’s honest, documented history. But it’s a different casualty from the nation, and the two blur together too easily. Even on its own terms, the pacing fails its nerve. The security hearing eats up the runtime; the actual moral reckoning gets compressed into mood and sound design instead of a position the film is willing to hold. A question this big — was this justified? — can’t be answered by half. Beautiful score, exceptional editing, a flawless cast. None of it amounts to an argument.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Oppenheimer is a technically extraordinary film that ultimately keeps its most serious question at arm's length. It flirts with self-criticism through the psychology of one man while leaving the nation's — and the weapon's — actual victims outside the frame entirely. Craft of this level deserves an equally serious answer to the question it raises, not an atmosphere of unease standing in for one.

Un film che conferma la mia opinione su Nolan, incredibile operatore di macchina ma autore scadente. Da un punto di vista tecnico il film è eccellente, ci sono scene (auditorium) incredibili che sicuramente segneranno visivamente la storia del cinema. Ciò detto il film è vuoto, non all’altezza delle aspettative che aveva creato, paradossalmente tanto superficiale quanto Barbie (2023). Sembra una poesia barocca, straripante di artifici retorici ma povera di contenuto. Nolan non si preoccupa di scrivere dialoghi comprensibili a chi non ha studiato fisica quantistica, non si ferma mai a spiegare gli esperimenti, vengono nominati personaggi quasi solo per il gusto di inserire quanti più scienziati possibili, come se per il pubblico generalista (a cui questo film è inevitabilmente rivolto) fossero informazioni scontate. In un certo senso è elitario, serve per far gongolare quei quattro dotti che riescono a cogliere questa o quella citazione al mondo della ricerca scientifica del XX secolo (esattamente come fanno i film Marvel, mi dispiace ma è così). Nolan non ha il coraggio di parlare veramente della bomba nucleare. Non gli interessa veramente parlare della bomba nucleare. Gli interessa far vedere le esplosioni e quanto bene riesce a ricrearle. La strage dell’atomico si riassume in frasi dette in stanzini delle élite, i morti sono solo numeri. “Ma non è questo di cui parla il film!!!!!” Ah si parliamo di Robert Oppenheimer. Dopo TRE ORE di film cosa sappiamo di lui? Niente. Lui è sconvolto, fine. Murphy fa facce basite per tutto il film, il suo personaggio sembra trascendere la realtà che lo circonda, non è presente ma sempre richiuso nella sua testa. Cosa ne pensa della bomba? Lo rifarebbe? È stata ambizione? Passione per la ricerca? Lui ogni tanto dubita, ma fa le cose che fa perché gli vengono ordinate. Fine. Sembra neurodivergente per come si pone di fronte alle autorità e alle relazioni. È incapace di mostrare sentimenti autentici, sembra un robot. Dei suoi sentimenti non viene fuori nulla, solo vaghe sensazioni. È più sviluppato il personaggio di Strauss (un incredibile Robert D Junior) di cui abbiamo in meno minutaggio un’introspezione più completa. Questo film non fa riflettere. L’ultima scena è bella, ma oltre a “wow” perché Nolan sceglie le inquadrature giuste non rimane niente. Non prende posizione. Non ha il coraggio di esprimere un’opinione. Non ti lascia niente. Finisce il film, spegni la tv e vai avanti con la tua vita, “ah sì forse oppenheimer era comunista, non lo sapevo, bello però il mondo in fiamme”. Per quanto mi riguarda le grandi opere dovrebbero toccarti nel profondo e cambiarti la vita, altrimenti sono solo distrazioni ben confezionate.

I’m still yet to see The Odyssey, but it’s basically impossible to read anything related to film right now and not find an essay on how Christoper Nolan has finally completed his accidental reverse  triptych on tracing the evolution of man's relationship to power and evil, on the heroes who mistake intelligence for virtue. The Odyssey imagines the mythic birth of strategic violence, to be cunning is to acquire the status of a moral good. Tenet imagines something much later and much more bleak, the bureaucratisation of the apocalypse. While Oppenheimer is found somewhere in the middle, the shift from strategy to science, the genius who acquires the capacity to destroy the world. History, read backwards, starts to echo a series of increasingly sophisticated excuses of exceptional men. It’s a very stylish and neat way to view the films, more stylish and neat, perhaps, then the films themselves. And while these film’s three leads, Odysseus, Oppenheimer, and the Protagonist may be from different centuries, experiencing different crises, each man crosses a threshold that cannot be uncrossed, each inheriting history itself as both burden and the very justification for existence.  And I don’t know if I fully agree, Nolan doesn’t quite seem the type of filmmaker to spend over a decade silently remaking the same film; but the reading makes one thing feel clear to me, that Oppenheimer is much more a clear symptom of Nolan’s work than his masterpiece. I’m not exactly a fan of Tenet, a film less intellectually rigorous than hermetically sealed, so completely fascinated by its own narrative mechanisms, smugly constructing its timeloop as an axiom, that it never stops to ask if it is mistaking opacity for complexity. For a film that is supposed to feel like human agency is being dissolved into infrastructure, it’s strangely legible, the end was always written into the beginning, it all makes sense in the end, there’s always a hero to its story, even if we only see the consequences of actions already chosen. If I wanted cinema like that then I’d much rather take Assayas’s Demonlover, or Denis’s Bastards every time, at least those films see something Nolan never can bring into sight; those systems become frightening because no one can comprehend them. The very forms of those films do not ask us to admire their architectures, but they ask us to live inside the consequences, never becoming legible because the modern world does not allow for it; these are stories of networks, not heroes. But with Oppenheimer I find my feelings more disjointed; it doesn’t help that the public reaction to the film seems to proclaim it as the grand brilliant masterpiece to define the 2020s American cinema. It’s obviously an accomplished film on most technical levels, and I can appreciate a lot of it’s editing, and a genuine fantastic lead performance; but any admiration I have turns to stone by the time its greatest irony has come to light; a film about the invention of systems capacity of escaping our control (nuclear winter) is so convinced that history is driven by the great man. How can one singular consciousness make us feel the weight of such horrors? The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings show up not as straight realities but as subjective events that disturb Oppenheimer’s own interior life. Is the film refusal to depict these events an ethical one to stop atrocity turning into aesthetics? I’m not convinced, we leave so much knowing about what it feels to invent the bomb, but we feel so little about what that means for… everyone else, including those who lived beneath it. The limits of making a biopic about a man’s guilt is failing to be a statement on how humanity doomed itself with his invention, you either make us understand catastrophe, or how it feels to be ‘great’ but ‘cursed’. Nolan’s films have always been fascinated by guilt, exceptional men have to be crushed eventually by the weight of their exceptional decisions, too heavy for ‘normal people’ to understand; but guilt is not morality, and Nolan’s guilt more resembles proof of one’s exceptional depth than functioning as their own ethical reckoning. Oppenheimer must suffer so intensely through his mind that his suffering becomes the film’s moral inquiry. Are we ‘really’ confronting evil? Or just watching a man’s conscience work as usual? (I feel like those TikToks about men where it’s like ‘men are just now having the thoughts we have at a sleepover at nine’). Again and again, in Nolan’s cinema, civilisation persists because one extraordinary man discovers that one’s intelligence can allow them to suspend morality. Splitting the atom, the Trojan Horse, controlling time itself. Different myths that share the fundamental conviction, history depends on the men who act when everyone else cannot. But that’s the rancid conservative impulse at the heart of his filmmaking, maybe not quite in the partisan sense (although we’ve all seen the think pieces on Dark Knight and Interstellar), but in the shape of his histories. This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

And I don’t know if I fully agree, Nolan doesn’t quite seem the type of filmmaker to spend over a decade silently remaking the same film; but the reading makes one thing feel clear to me, that Oppenheimer is much more a clear symptom of Nolan’s work than his masterpiece. I’m not exactly a fan of Tenet, a film less intellectually rigorous than hermetically sealed, so completely fascinated by its own narrative mechanisms, smugly constructing its timeloop as an axiom, that it never stops to ask if it is mistaking opacity for complexity. For a film that is supposed to feel like human agency is being dissolved into infrastructure, it’s strangely legible, the end was always written into the beginning, it all makes sense in the end, there’s always a hero to its story, even if we only see the consequences of actions already chosen. If I wanted cinema like that then I’d much rather take Assayas’s Demonlover, or Denis’s Bastards every time, at least those films see something Nolan never can bring into sight; those systems become frightening because no one can comprehend them. The very forms of those films do not ask us to admire their architectures, but they ask us to live inside the consequences, never becoming legible because the modern world does not allow for it; these are stories of networks, not heroes. But with Oppenheimer I find my feelings more disjointed; it doesn’t help that the public reaction to the film seems to proclaim it as the grand brilliant masterpiece to define the 2020s American cinema. It’s obviously an accomplished film on most technical levels, and I can appreciate a lot of its editing, and a genuine fantastic lead performance; but any admiration I have turns to stone by the time its greatest irony has come to light; a film about the invention of systems capacity of escaping our control (nuclear winter) is so convinced that history is driven by the great man. How can one singular consciousness make us feel the weight of such horrors? The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings show up not as straight realities but as subjective events that disturb Oppenheimer’s own interior life. Is the film refusal to depict these events an ethical one to stop atrocity turning into aesthetics? I’m not convinced, we leave so much knowing about what it feels to invent the bomb, but we feel so little about what that means for… everyone else, including those who lived beneath it. The limits of making a biopic about a man’s guilt is failing to be a statement on how humanity doomed itself with his invention, you either make us understand catastrophe, or how it feels to be ‘great’ but ‘cursed’. Nolan’s films have always been fascinated by guilt, exceptional men have to be crushed eventually by the weight of their exceptional decisions, too heavy for ‘normal people’ to understand; but guilt is not morality, and Nolan’s guilt more resembles proof of one’s exceptional depth than functioning as their own ethical reckoning. Oppenheimer must suffer so intensely through his mind that his suffering becomes the film’s moral inquiry. Are we ‘really’ confronting evil? Or just watching a man’s conscience work as usual? (I feel like those TikToks about men where it’s like ‘men are just now having the thoughts we had at a sleepover at nine’). Again and again, in Nolan’s cinema, civilisation persists because one extraordinary man discovers that one’s intelligence can allow them to suspend morality. Splitting the atom, the Trojan Horse, controlling time itself. Different myths that share the fundamental conviction, history depends on the men who act when everyone else cannot. But that’s the rancid conservative impulse at the heart of his filmmaking, maybe not quite in the partisan sense (although we’ve all seen the think pieces on Dark Knight and Interstellar), but in the shape of his histories. This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

Oppenheimer est symptomatique de la filmographie de Cristopher Nolan. Il réinterprète des sujets passionnants et complexes avec des moyens colossaux et une capacité rare de créer un engouement massif auprès du grand public. Cependant, Oppenheimer, tout comme Interstellar ou Tenet, tombe toujours dans les mêmes travers qui font de ses œuvres des gâchis bien tristes. Des temporalités mélangées, où on aime faire des bonds dans le futur pour inlassablement revenir en arrière, des twists de merde artificiellement complexifiés et des personnages qui aiment s'écouter parler. Un cinéma "intelligent" ou un cinéma balourd qui impose à son public de se concentrer pendant 3 heures jusqu'à ne plus rien comprendre tant on est surchargés d'information pour se convaincre de la supériorité cérébrale de son scénario. Volontairement fatiguant, rien n'est développé si sa mise en scène ne sert pas l'histoire, le film passe son temps à expliquer ce qu'il ne filme pas. On apprend pas grand chose de Oppenheimer, de ce qu'il est, de ce qu'il fait, de ce qu'il le motive, de l'homme de science qu'il a été, de l'homme de pouvoir qu'il est devenu, de ses états d'âme, des conséquences de ses actions. Mais on préfère s'étendre sur un procès qui se passe on ne sait pas trop quand exactement, parce que Robert Downey Jr. est on se sait pas trop qui, qui souhaite empêcher à Cilian Murphy on ne sait pas trop quoi qui permettrait à ce dernier de faire quelque chose de sûrement important. Et c'est pas le film qui va nous aider à y voir beaucoup plus clair, profitant de la confusion pour mieux cacher les lacunes de Nolan. Au final, on finit par s'extasier sur le moindre acteur un peu connu ou sur des scènes bien américaines comme le namedrop de JFK vers la fin du film comme si c'était une scène post crédit Marvel. Mais peut-être que les histoires de cul intéressent plus Nolan que le tragique des bombardements atomiques d'Hiroshima et de Nagasaki dont tout semblait faux (et ce n'est pas la faute à Cilian Murphy) puisque le film n'avait cœur à rien. i'm gonna preface this with a warning that i've grown very disillusioned with christopher nolan as of late. i haven't lost affection for his films of which i am already fond, but i am a lot more aware of his shortcomings as a director now than i have historically been, and they bother me a lot more. honestly sometimes with all the glazing going on i feel like film enjoyers are under some kind of group psychosis about how talented the man is. buuuuut that is neither here nor there, because today i am here to talk about oppenheimer . i think i had a decently open mind going in, and the film got off to a good start. i mean, the thing hauls. from the very beginning, something is always happening. it left me feeling breathless, but eventually i realized it was not in a good way. it kinda just made me tired. i would've been impressed if it had maintained the momentum all the way through, but the endless repetition of "important" conversation after important conversation got old and then the momentum didn't matter anymore. each conversation felt like an event that needed to happen before the story could move along to the next. a sequence of interactions, each ending with a miniature mic-drop, that communicated information but didn't say anything interesting. i took a note that compared this constant vapid go-go-go to my own tendency to play music 24/7 to distract myself from everything, including and especially my own interiority. i know it's an unfulfilling and terribly un-present way to live, but it avoids most discomfort. this film is largely the same! rapid pace & perpetual talking unsuccessfully try to distract from the fact that nothing weighty is being discussed. we're talking about the invention & use of the atomic bomb, for fricks sake, and i basically just dissociated under the impression of a meaningful movie for three hours. there are a couple scenes that made me think it was about to pivot in a more interesting & resonant direction—the meeting to decide if/where to drop the bombs on japan (perfectly sickening), and the conference with oppenheimer speaking to los alamos about the bombs' "performance", to name two—but then we were right back in a series of important conversations. too little, too late. so if it's not about the effects of the bomb... what is this about? the title suggests the subject is the man, but i didn't even become familiar enough with him to understand him, much less identify with him. his infidelity is either easily glossed over or played for laughs. his reaction to the impending loss of his q-clearance seems a bigger loss than his bombs dropped on nagasaki & hiroshima. idk man. what are we doing here. specific nolan-isms i noticed in this film — he loves a blameless martyr of a man. a man who is as much a product of his circumstances, his era, his society as he is tortured by them. i often do this with my d&d characters, so i understand the appeal. but dude... at what point does this go beyond a preference and into an inability to deal with actual nuance? or moral grayness? i hear odysseus is given the same treatment and i personally think that's an unforgivable way to mangle him beyond recognition — everything feels so... inhuman. the interpersonal relationships are lacking—why did jean & kitty even like this guy? why is einstein reduced to the wise old wizard role?—and i even felt alienated from oppenheimer himself (see above). — loud ≠ emotionally powerful. the score itself is good, but i don't think it's very well-utilized. it's wielded like a cudgel at times and those instances of dramatic loudness just felt like heavy-handed (and wholly unsuccessful) attempts at emotional manipulation. disappointing

Revisiting Nolan #12: ‘Oppenheimer’ gets a lot of praise that I didn’t understand when I left the theatre. I was somewhat bored by this incredible interesting subject. Alas, I still think this isn’t all that. While Nolan sure knows how to capture a movie on film his non-linear shenanigans kills every momentum. This structure works for some of his movies (Memento, The Prestige), but not for all. On top of that I really hated the fragmented storytelling as well. Not one scene plays, for what feels like, longer than 1 minute tops. It doesn’t enhance the viewing experience, it makes it an exhausting one. I also don’t really have the feeling that I know Oppie, or any of the other characters as well because of it. It doesn’t make me find them interesting, which doesn’t make me care about any of them, which makes me not invested in any of them. It just turns me off in so many ways. The movie is also way too long. After the 40th interrogation/hearing scene I just about had it and really thought this could’ve used a 40-45 minute trimming. I’m so sad the newer output of Nolan doesn’t appear to appeal to me anymore. I really loved his work and still can’t deny his craftsmanship as a director. Visually his movies are amazing, he gets top notch performances from his cast, his movies will stand the test of time as he goes as much practical as he can,… List goes on and on. But, I also can’t deny he’s boring the shit out of me and can’t quite hold my attention anymore. People compare this with Stone’s ‘JFK’, and I get and see that, but that movie is a million times better than this.

Unfortunately Oppenheimer was exactly as I suspected it would be: Lots of intellectual dick-swinging and acting/dialogue that is generally bland and cold as unseasoned, leftover chicken breast with not much actual artistry or depth. Nolan’s filmmaking style in general doesn’t do much for me despite my efforts to appreciate it more. It's lots of shiny spectacle and technicality with some awkward editing peppered throughout and an at times overpowering and distracting score. As per usual ( Interstellar aside) not a single character resonated with me emotionally. Even Oppenheimer himself as an antihero didn’t really reach me on a human level. What exactly was I supposed to feel here? I will say that it's far more visually compelling in regards to the cinematography and color grading than The Odyssey , and I think it also features some of Nolan's strongest casting choices (I am prepared to die on this hill). A major gripe I have though is that once again the women only exist to propel, serve and revolve around the male characters. As critic Angelica Jade Bastién has stated, “Nolan’s genius ends when a woman enters the frame.” Regardless of whether or not he’s actually misogynist I can’t help but feel as if his films generally come across that way, even if it really is unintentional. Florence Pugh (Jean Tatlock) seems to only exist as an empty and tragic sexual reprieve from all of the overwrought exposition. Emily Blunt (Kitty Oppenheimer) plays a neglected wife and mother who’s reduced to anger, tears, and alcoholism. Little empathy is shown to either, neither of them really have any agency. Also why was there not more Lilli Hornig (Olivia Thirlby)? Or Charlotte Serber (Jessica Erin Martin)? There are so many opportunities for Nolan to really expand and empower the women in his films, yet he consistently falls short. If someone goes in knowing very little or nothing at all about the subject matter then it's a decent depiction of the Manhattan Project and Oppenheimer as a person. But if you’re already well-versed in the lore--and aren’t a history buff who simply loves anything in relation to it--save yourself the time and energy by watching Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove instead. I'd personally rather watch a razor-sharp satire about the catastrophic potential of the atomic age that is as funny as it is well-acted (and it’s only 95 minutes)! Some (superficial) highlights: - Cillian Murphy being Cillian Murphy (i.e. a stone cold fox). - The casting of David "I've got a dick on my face, don't I?" Krumholtz (iykyk). - Roughly six minutes of Florence Pugh (I love her and I'll take what I can get). - Josh Hartnett giving Harrison Ford in Raiders of the Lost Ark vibes with those slutty little glasses (he's truly aged like a fine wine).

"When I came to you with those calculations, we thought we might start a chain reaction that would destroy the entire world." Oppenheimer is a movie with a message... but the message is far more memorable than the movie itself. Make no mistake: Christopher Nolan's film, which won seven Academy Awards including best picture and best director, is an impressive technical milestone, particularly for its score, sound design, and maybe editing. I say "maybe" editing because though Jennifer Lame has overall succeeded in condensing an encyclopedia of information into a three hour film and making it (mostly) involving, the story is extremely hard to follow. Not just sequences, but individual scenes look disjointed. There may have been a stronger sense of setup and payoff if the footage was differently arranged, and better shot (more on that later). I also wonder how much of the material we actually needed to understand the film's main point, which is that the invention of a divinely powerful weapon will destroy the world in one way or another. The first two hours of the film detail the creation and testing of the atomic bomb, while the last hour focuses on Admiral Strauss manipulating the 1954 Gray Board hearing to ruin Oppenheimer's reputation. This latter event felt extremely petty and trivial in comparison to the tragedies of World War II, but as the final scene reveals, maybe that was the point. Strauss's egotism is like a bomb that, when ignited, wrecks the dignity of those who are the unfortunate target. But I still did not care about this subplot, despite it being historically accurate (I think), and I would have been more interested in the drama between Oppenheimer and his former assistant, Edward Teller. Then there is Nolan's typical lack of camera direction; most of the dialogue scenes (which constitute maybe 90 percent of the film) simply cut back and forth between actors who dump exposition and scientific formulas in monotonous voices in front of plain-looking backgrounds. Films like Inception are similarly guilty, but Nolan's best films are often redeemed by his imaginative premises (e.g. a dream within a dream). But once Nolan began to direct stories that weren't his own, his films - at least for me - lost their flavor. It is the main criticism that I have against The Odyssey and, to a marginally lesser extent, Oppenheimer . Nevertheless, Oppenheimer forces viewers to think critically about the moral implications of using such dangerous weapons at will. Should we play with fire just because we can? It is an extremely important message in today's world, and that alone makes the film worth watching at least once. As a piece of entertainment, however, the film falters. This was my third viewing, and I still zoned out several times throughout the movie. Most people seem to love Oppenheimer , but for me, it does not "take in the sheets."

This is my third time watching this film, and it gets better with every watch. From the moment the opening frame of raindrops shows, I was captivated. The rain being a motif for the consequences and troubles of Oppenheimer is a beautiful decision, and it executed perfectly throughout the entire film. It shows the weight that Oppenheimer has to carry with the decisions that he made, even if he appears to not be fully set on his emotions. Murphy absolutely deserved the Oscar for this masterful, career-defining performance. The way he able to play an anti-hero by showing regret through his voice and emotional restraint at times is done in a way only a few actors can do. I’d like to applaud the successful writing as well. Oppenheimer is one of the most complex characters Nolan has written. He has many moral flaws throughout, and even more contradictions to his actions, but yet the audience is made to feel for him emotionally, as we see the weight he carries, and the regret he holds, even if it’s too late. The cinematography in this film is also superb. The use of frequent, quick flashes throughout helps create the overall story, and sets the tone for what is going on. It allows for complex story telling, well-rounded characters, and sophisticated story telling. This helps create the great structure and pacing that this film has, which many argue is a problem in other Nolan movies. I can’t write this review without giving praise to Ludwig, and his amazing score for this film. It’s his best work, and I think he’ll have a hard time ever topping this string carried melody. I’d also like to shoutout Emily blunt. Her performance is already very famous for what she does with such little screen time, but the praise is warranted. Her face acting is a masterclass in show don’t tell. If she had more screen time, she’d have an Oscar for this role, which she might’ve deserved even with the little time she had to show off her talent. This is Nolan’s second best film. It has become very clear to me after debating this for a long time. This watch was necessary for me to determine where this ranks in his filmography. It is also the best film of the 2020s so far. There’s an argument for Dune 2, but Oppenheimer still clears. Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds.

Wanted to check that my perception of this film was not clouded by me being 17 and fairly new to IMAX at release. Those checks have cleared. The greatest lead acting performance ever. Greatest VFX and SFX ever, and would-be greatest score if Ludwig didn’t top it with Sinners. The perfection of Nolan’s exposition and weird editing of dialogue panning to everyone but the speaker’s face. Everyone involved in this film was born to play their role in it. The build and release of tension (much like how the movie presents fission) is masterful, using gorgeous visuals of subatomic warfare and sonic booms of egotism to represent the fractured genius of Oppenheimer’s mind and conscience in both the physical and moral sense in the lead-up, execution and conclusion of his most important moments. The Trinity Test remains my favourite scene ever crafted. What separates this from other biopics, or even The Odyssey, is the ambiguity that Nolan allows the viewer to cherish. Your view of Oppenheimer’s morality and consequentiality is entirely up to your reading of events - with clear view of the Red Scare, of America’s myths, of human history; you are the jury.

I remember when my Grandmother used to speak with me on the phone about Harry Truman's speech indicating the end of World War II. She would start to tear up when he spoke about how not one more American would be killed. It used to be very powerful to hear. There was, however, a missing part of this story I never knew about, the man who had to live with creating the bomb that ended the war. The film takes us from the opening credits to the kangaroo court of J. Robert Oppenheimer. Due to his past associations with communists, he never stood a chance. It was amazing to watch his brilliance be taken over by a man who was no more loyal to him than the communists he once befriended. Oppenheimer was the main architect who built the atomic bomb and he lived with the guilt long after it dropped. This guilt and a petty grudge gave Lewis Strauss all the ammunition he needed. Strauss got what he wanted from Oppenheimer. Strauss takes down Oppenheimer by sticking him in a kangaroo court. Afterwards, Strauss doesn't realize he's sitting in his own version of a kangaroo court until it's too late. I remember walking out of the theater and my friend and I both agreed how amazing it was. In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan used IMAX cameras for the entire film. In Oppenheimer, he used them for a majority of the film. This made it a visual spectacle that looked as good on a 4K TV as it did when I saw it in theaters. Cillian Murphy was an actor I knew of before this film. As Oppenheimer, he became the emotional center of the film regardless of time or destination. I could look in his eyes and know the highs and lows of being the man who received far more credit than he wanted. Beyond Nolan's directing, my friend and I discussed Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss extensively. I thought he was going to have a good chance at winning the Oscar, but he stole the film in every scene he was in. I saw Oppenheimer 3 years ago on the anniversary of the bomb dropping in Hiroshima in 1945. It was a moment that hit me after I left the theater. A few weeks later, I watched the film again in theaters, and then a few months later again with my Mom. Each time I thought to myself about how Oppenheimer had to live with what he did. Lewis Strauss had to live with unnecessary pettiness that cost him what he worked so hard for. Harry Truman may have taken responsibility, but guilt has to fall on someone's shoulders. Oppenheimer wasn't wrong for taking on the guilt, but just like his other mistakes, decisions are very hard to take back once they've been made.
